source_title: Marriott International, Inc. - Form 10-K and Q4/Full-Year 2020 Results (Fiscal Year 2020)
publisher_issuer: Marriott International, Inc. (filed with U.S. SEC, EDGAR CIK 0001048286; corroborated by Marriott Q4 2020 earnings release)
company_context: Marriott International is the world's largest hotel company, operating an asset-light franchise/management model. COVID-19 caused an unprecedented collapse in global lodging demand in 2020, forcing Marriott into aggressive liquidity preservation to bridge the demand trough.
macro_context: COVID-19 pandemic; global travel restrictions and lockdowns drove worldwide RevPAR down roughly two-thirds, the most severe demand shock in the hotel industry's history.
evidence_summary: COVID-19 cut Marriott's full-year 2020 total revenues to $10,571 million (from prior peak levels) and produced a net loss of $267 million; fourth-quarter 2020 worldwide comparable systemwide RevPAR fell 64.1%. Marriott preserved liquidity by drawing on its $4.5 billion credit facility, issuing $3.6 billion of senior notes, suspending its dividend and share repurchases on March 18, 2020, obtaining a leverage-covenant waiver through Q1 2021, and raising ~$920 million via loyalty-program amendments. It ended 2020 with about $4.4 billion of net liquidity (~$0.8B cash plus ~$3.6B undrawn revolver) and survived the shock.
owner_decision_context: Facing a near-total collapse in lodging demand, management chose to maximize liquidity and financial flexibility rather than risk a covenant breach or cash exhaustion: draw the revolver, issue notes, halt shareholder returns, negotiate a covenant waiver, and monetize the loyalty program.
action_taken: Suspended dividend and buybacks (3/18/2020), borrowed under the $4.5B credit facility, issued $3.6B of senior notes, secured a leverage-covenant waiver through Q1 2021, and raised ~$920M through loyalty-program amendments, ending 2020 with ~$4.4B net liquidity.
outcome_evidence: Despite a $267M net loss and a 64.1% Q4 RevPAR collapse, Marriott maintained ~$4.4B of net liquidity at year-end 2020, reduced Q4 debt by more than $600M, avoided distress default, and recovered as travel rebounded, confirming a temporary-shock-with-recovery outcome.
source_limitations: WebFetch of sec.gov and the PR Newswire earnings release returned HTTP 403; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to Marriott's FY2020 10-K / Q4 2020 earnings release (revenues $10,571M, net loss $267M, $4.5B facility, $3.6B notes, $920M loyalty cash, $4.4B liquidity, 64.1% RevPAR, 3/18/2020 suspension). Full annual RevPAR decline and exact peak-year revenue were not separately confirmed and are omitted.
directly_stated: Marriott reported a net loss of $267 million for 2020
Q4 2020 worldwide comparable systemwide RevPAR declined 64.1%
Marriott borrowed under its $4.5 billion credit facility and issued $3.6 billion of senior notes
Marriott suspended its dividend and share repurchases on March 18, 2020
Marriott obtained a leverage-covenant waiver through Q1 2021 and raised ~$920 million via loyalty-program amendments
Year-end 2020 net liquidity was approximately $4.4 billion
inferred: The bundle of liquidity actions, not operating performance, is what carried Marriott through the demand trough
The asset-light model amplified the revenue collapse but also limited fixed costs, aiding survival
why_useful_for_opsiq: Clean example of a fundamentally healthy business hit by an exogenous macro shock that responds with a governed liquidity-preservation playbook (draw revolver, issue notes, suspend returns, waive covenant) and survives. Tests whether the engine classifies the condition as temporary shock requiring liquidity defense rather than a structural failure, and whether it credits covenant-waiver and shareholder-return suspension as appropriate phase-correct actions.
